newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Sexual revolution afoot in Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Sexual revolution afoot in Cambodia.

text.p: A two-year study has shattered the traditionally chaste image of Cambodia's young women and raised serious concerns about the spread of AIDS among the country's youth.
The Cambodian AIDS Social Research Project found that roughly one-third of young women are sexually active in this traditionally restrictive culture, but none use condoms, researchers said this week.
About 87 percent of young men are having sex with their girlfriends, prostitutes or -- in the case of 10 percent of the subjects -- with other males.
But nearly half of sexually active men never use a condom, despite the fact that Cambodia has one of Asia's fastest growing infection rates of HIV, the study said.
The results signal that a social revolution is taking place among Cambodia's young, who comprise more than half of the population, researchers said.
"The enthnographic data our young researchers have managed to generate is truly quite shocking," Chou Meng Tarr, the Cambodian lead researcher for the study, wrote in her report.
"I am still very shocked with the findings as they appear to be completely at variance with everything I thought possible in my own society," she wrote.

Peter Aggleton, coordinator of the project and head of the Thomas Coran Reasearch Unit at the University of London, recently said the study could mean more than 380,000 young women and 878,000 young men are engaged in risky sexual behaviour.
An estimated 90,000 to 120,000 people in Cambodia have HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), the virus that causes the incurable AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome).
The study, released to Reuters this week, was conducted by high-school and university students trained as researchers in an effort to encourage candour among their peers, Chou Meng Tarr said.

The researchers held discussions with 281 young people ranging from ages 14 to 26 over the course of 22 months. The subjects included a cross-section of rural and urban youth from varying backgrounds.
But Chou Meng Tarr cautioned that the study was more valuable for its insight into sexual behaviour than as a statistically valid source of data.
The study was funded by the Geneva-based World Health Organisation, which has conducted similar studies in Africa and Latin America.

Chou Meng Tarr told Reuters the gap between traditional Cambodian values and the sexual behaviour of youth revealed a problem with existing AIDS education programmes: they do not involve youth and are more geared to men and sex workers.
"We need to involve young people in public education and discuss sexual behaviour in the media," she said. "Without the active involvement of young peole, we cannot...stop the spread of AIDS."
